summary_md:
Malaterre and Lareau (Data & Policy 6, e5, 2024) is a proof of concept for finding "hidden communities of interest" (HCoIs) when no tie data exist. They fit a 25-topic LDA to 16,917 philosophy-of-science articles (1930-2017). They average each author's topic shares within each of four roughly 21-year periods. Authors with more than 2 weighted publications are kept, which leaves at most 8,009 authors. Authors are linked when the Pearson correlation of their profiles is at least 0.6, and Louvain then finds communities. Communities in adjacent periods are matched by Hellinger distance to trace their history. Over time, modularity rises (0.427 to 0.834), density falls (0.167 to 0.030), and the number of communities goes from 4 to 13. The only validation is that the results agree with the known history of the field. The authors also say plainly that HCoI ties are mediated by text and are a heuristic for possible real ties, not social ties. They argue the method suits policy text but do not test it on any.

For Paul's systems this paper is not new: it is the stated source of fec/network/press_hcoi.py, built on 2026-07-01. That script copies the pipeline almost step for step, except that it uses 19 regex-tagged CU press categories in place of LDA topics. Two system findings back the authors' own caveat. First, the HCoI layer was null for stance co-movement (49%). Second, it recovered only 4 of 41 cosponsor-isolated members. The paper therefore supports building the layer, but it does not support reading HCoIs as coalitions, as closeness, or as influence channels. Those are the readings the system's assumption text, Paul's annotation, and the holistic edge admission lean toward. Everything here is a single-agent reading and is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Pipeline: LDA k=25 on 16,917 articles; per-author, per-period topic profiles weighted by authorship share; keep authors with weighted publications > 2; Pearson correlation >= 0.6; Louvain (Gephi default); community profile = mean of member profiles; genealogy by closest Hellinger pairing between adjacent ~21-year periods. bearings.paper_location: Section 2.2 p.6-9; Section 3.1-3.2 p.9-14; Table 3 p.10; Fig. 9 p.13
bearings.system_side: press_hcoi.py copies the pipeline but swaps the LDA topics for 19 curated, regex-tagged press categories. Each item's weight is split evenly across its labels and weighted by recency. It keeps the same r >= 0.6 cutoff (HCOI_CORR), uses MIN_W 3.0 as its version of '>2', runs Louvain once with seed 7, and drops communities with fewer than 3 members. Profiles are weighted by member. History is a single median-date split into two periods, and each period-2 community is matched to its closest period-1 community by Hellinger distance. The PERSISTS / drifts / NOVEL labels use cutoffs of 0.25 and 0.45 that the script invented; they are not in the paper.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The mechanics carry over directly. The paper's evidence does not: it covers an 88-year academic corpus in four periods, where more than 80% of authors are new each period, and its validation is qualitative only. Paul's corpus is one domain-scoped press stream (2022-01..2026-06) split into two periods, so a 'NOVEL' or 'PERSISTS' label reflects the script's own thresholds, not anything the paper showed. The paper also gives no guidance on running Louvain with one seed versus several.

bearings.paper_claim: HCoIs are about who talks about the same things as whom. The links are mediated by texts, are not social ties, and serve only as a heuristic for possible real ties. Communities are labelled from topic profiles, not from alignment.
bearings.system_side: The component assumes that shared issue attention indicates a coalition and attributes that to Malaterre and Lareau. The profiles are shares of attention with no stance sign: categories are counted without the stance column. As a result, a community such as H-5 (CU-Bank+CCM 'defensive-fight talkers') can hold members on both sides of the same fight. The system's own co-movement test on HCoI same-community pairs was null (49%).
bearings.transfer_conditions: This carries over fully, because it is a definitional limit of the method, not a property of the sample. An HCoI is a topical-attention measure (who talks about what), not an alignment measure (which side they take). Reading it as a coalition requires a signed profile (attention times stance), which neither the paper nor the code builds.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper offers no evidence that text-similarity ties carry influence or transmission. It frames HCoI mapping as a heuristic for real ties that would still need confirmation.
bearings.system_side: build_multilayer_network admits HCoI correlation edges into the cascade kernel at weight 0.6 x r x HCOI_W, capped at 0.12 (p about 0.02 per step). Under the CU config only edges touching a cosponsor-isolated member are admitted (4 of 41 reconnected). Under the holistic configs the 'dominance' rule (Paul ruling 2026-08-18) admits them in general: HCoI edges went from 0 to 857, and a tied pair takes max(cosponsor, media).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Using HCoI edges as a low-weight reachability patch for leadership members, who do not cosponsor by norm, is consistent with the paper's 'heuristic' framing. Treating them as transmission edges in cascade, coalition, or route outputs goes beyond what the paper tested. Any output that depends on them must say it rests on a topical-similarity heuristic.

bearings.paper_claim: HCoI ties come from thematic similarity of texts, not from relationships or shared positions. The method says nothing about agreement or change in agreement.
bearings.system_side: stance_dynamics runs a neighbour co-movement test on HCoI same-community pairs and finds a null result (49%). Its imputation proposals use only cosponsor-graph neighbours (at least 5 neighbours and |estimate| >= 0.75) and never use HCoI neighbours.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The null result is what the paper's construct predicts: similar topic attention says nothing about stance movement. This supports keeping the HCoI layer out of stance imputation. It says nothing about whether cosponsor-based imputation works.

bearings.paper_claim: k is chosen by combining Cv coherence (scanned over k = 5-100, with no gain above 35) and manual reading of top words. Any topic model works as long as topic assignments are continuous probabilities rather than crisp. Topics depend on the corpus and unit of analysis.
bearings.system_side: The HCoI profile input is the regex category tagging: 19 categories, each item assigned crisp labels split evenly. The precision of that tagging against human coding has never been measured, and no coherence or overlap check exists for the categories.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's continuous-assignment requirement holds only loosely: member profiles are continuous after aggregation, but each item is tagged crisply. A cheap check would be either a coherence-selected LDA on the same press corpus or a precision sample of the regex tags. That would show whether the communities reflect the taxonomy or the text. Any such result stays a diagnostic until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: The quality of an HCoI network depends on how representative the corpus is, and this is crucial for any conclusion. The authors flag the venues and languages they left out.
bearings.system_side: The collector caps each member at 1000 URLs, prioritised by CU-term titles. Recorded coverage is uneven: D 92.5% vs R 87%, and Senate 83% vs House 96%. Which members are profiled (MIN_W 3.0) and placed in communities therefore depends on collection coverage.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The caution applies directly. Before HCoI membership or the D4 recovery count (4 of 41) is read substantively, check for party or chamber gaps in who gets profiled. Any figure should name its window (2022-01..2026-06) and its denominator (members profiled, not 533).

bearings.paper_claim: Communities in adjacent periods are matched by Hellinger distance between their profiles. This traces persistence, splits, and novel communities; for example, four novel communities appear in 1974-95.
bearings.system_side: Ward.D2 clustering on z-scored category-lean profiles, with lean weighted 3.0, minimum 6 members and 9 blocs. It is a static snapshot, its stability over time is an open question, and all blocs are mislabelled as pro-CU.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The genealogy step would answer the open stability question if the Ward blocs were re-run per period and matched by Hellinger distance. Unlike HCoIs, these blocs include stance lean, so a genealogy here would track alignment rather than attention alone. It is a weak bearing: the paper's evidence base for the step is qualitative.

gaps_exposed: The HCoI layer has never been checked against a quantitative criterion. The open question of whether press-attention communities predict within-community cosponsorship above chance has not been answered. The paper also validates only qualitatively, so it offers no bar to borrow.

There is no signed HCoI variant (attention times stance sign). The current communities cannot tell allies from opponents who fight over the same issue, such as the H-5 CU-Bank defensive-fight cluster.

The 19-category regex taxonomy that feeds the profiles has no measured precision and no counterpart to the paper's coherence-based choice of k. The paper's requirement that topic assignments be continuous is only partly met, because each item's tags are crisp and split evenly.

The genealogy uses one median-date split into two periods, with PERSISTS / drifts / NOVEL cutoffs (0.25 / 0.45) that are not anchored in the paper. There is also no member-overlap check alongside the profile distance.
Louvain runs once with a single seed (7), and there is no seed or resolution stability check on the 8 communities.
There is no representativeness audit of who gets profiled (MIN_W 3.0) by party or chamber, even though collection coverage differs (D 92.5 vs R 87%; Senate 83 vs House 96%).
flags: The component's assumption text, 'Shared issue attention indicates coalition (Malaterre & Lareau 2024)', overstates the paper. The paper says HCoI ties are mediated by text, are not social ties, and are only a heuristic for possible real ties. Under D-025, HCoI communities and edges must be described as topical-similarity heuristics, never as coalition, closeness, or access.

Paul's takeaway, 'infer closeness between two congressional offices from co-occurrence or textual similarity', uses closeness language that D-025 bars and that the paper itself disclaims. A safer wording is 'topical-similarity heuristic between offices'.

Paul's note that the paper 'explicitly applies the method to advocacy' is not accurate. The paper argues the method could apply to policy and advocacy, but it tests only a philosophy-of-science corpus.

Under the holistic configs, the dominance admission rule (Paul's 2026-08-18 ruling) puts 857 HCoI similarity edges into the cascade kernel. The paper gives no evidence that such ties transmit influence. This is flagged as beyond the paper's evidence, not as a recommendation to reverse the ruling.
The PERSISTS / drifts / NOVEL genealogy labels come from the system's own thresholds, not from the paper. Treat them as UNVERIFIED descriptive labels (DE-062).
Caution when quoting the paper: its text says betweenness, cohesion and modularity all increase, but cohesion in Table 3 is not monotone. Quote the table values, not the prose.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so neither rejected SNA proposal is implicated. LDA identity sources are also not involved.
paul_alignment: Paul's annotation agrees with the paper on method: shared semantic content becomes vectors, then correlation edges, then Louvain, with a time element. The system put this in place on 2026-07-01 (fec/network/press_hcoi.py) as a two-period Hellinger genealogy, so his note is stale. It still reads as a future extension, but it is built, and it has since produced two results his notes do not record. HCoI neighbours showed null stance co-movement (49%), and the layer reconnected only 4 of 41 cosponsor-isolated members under the CU config. His idea of a domain-specific topic model per trade association or client was carried out in a different form: a curated 19-category CU taxonomy instead of a per-client LDA, and that taxonomy has never been validated. Two parts of his reading go beyond the paper. One is the framing of office 'closeness', which conflicts with D-025 and with the authors' own heuristic caveat. The other is the claim that the paper 'applies' the method to advocacy, when it only argues that it could. His note that the authors 'slimmed down the articles' is partly right. Their efficiency comes from part-of-speech and frequency filtering of the lexicon, and from working with three small matrices instead of 8,009 semantic matrices.

related.why: Paul cross-references both papers for Louvain community detection on policy and legislative networks. Ardekani builds communities from relational and legislative structure, while Malaterre builds them from text similarity alone.

Both promise 'hidden' groupings. Aref's signed-network partition encodes agreement and disagreement, which is exactly the alignment signal that stance-blind HCoI attention profiles lack. Its system counterpart is melange-sna.signed-coalitions.
Pritoni reviews what actually drives lobbying coalitions (issue salience, brokers). That is the coalition theory the HCoI-as-coalition assumption would need, and Malaterre does not supply it.

Zhou models stance change on interaction graphs. The system's HCoI co-movement null shows that topical-similarity graphs do not stand in for the communication ties that kind of stance-dynamics modelling assumes.

Both treat politicians' text as relational data. Malaterre supplies the topic-to-community step, and Steinert-Threlkeld supplies the data-collection and representativeness concerns the HCoI layer inherits.
Kim builds communities from lobbying network structure. Malaterre builds them from text alone, so the two give independent community partitions that could be compared on the same members.

backlinks.why: Paul's position on frame-alignment cites both. Malaterre infers shared-attention communities from text (press HCoI), while Joo measures shared frames by duplication. Both rest on press text and have the same source-author attribution exposure.
Both infer ties from Pearson correlation of profile vectors (Malaterre with topic profiles at a 0.6 threshold, used in press_hcoi.py). Zareie anchors the correlation on direct common neighbours.
Source of the HCoI shared-issue-attention layer, one of the layers whose added value Baptista's overlap and ablation logic would test.

Malaterre builds communities from text-profile similarity (correlation, then a 0.6 threshold, then Louvain). Haythornthwaite's relational view says structure comes from observed relationships, and block modelling correlates tie profiles, not attribute profiles. The tension bears directly on how press HCoI should be interpreted.
Both threshold a correlation graph and run Louvain to find communities. Malaterre supplies the 0.6 threshold press_hcoi.py actually uses. Zhang uses 0.1 on burst vectors and gives no validation.
